newsitem.title: TURKEY: Troubled Turkish coalition clears censure hurdle.
newsitem.headline: Troubled Turkish coalition clears censure hurdle.

text.p: Turkey's embattled Islamist-led coalition on Tuesday survived a censure motion vote in the face of a military challenge which has strained the unity of the ruling alliance.
"Putting the censure motion...on the agenda has been rejected," deputy speaker Yasin Hatiboglu said after announcing MPs had voted 272 to 265 in favour of dropping the motion.
Despite signs of dissent in the conservative wing of the alliance, government deputies voted in a show of unity to defend the narrow majority held by Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan.

Erbakan's coalition has faced mounting pressure after a warning from the military about increasing Islamist activities and signs of discontent from the conservative wing of the alliance led by Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller.
The leading opposition party, charging the government with giving civil servants unequal pay rises, proposed the motion before the weekend military warning to Erbakan.
Erbakan, secular Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, dug in his heels against the military challenge on Tuesday.
"Parliament gives the job of serving the nation to the government and the government is responsible only to parliament," he told a meeting of his Islam-based Welfare Party.
The military-dominated National Security Council has ordered Erbakan to reverse a recent wave of Islamist zeal in a warning that has shaken the country.

Istanbul stocks plunged more than 12 percent before clawing back to end the day down 5.19 percent, after a drop on Monday of 5.58 percent. Brokers said Tuesday's fall was due to poor inflation figures and mounting political worries.

The government cleared another hurdle later on Tuesday when MPs voted 274 to 258 against launching an inquiry into Justice Minister Sevket Kazan, a close aide of Erbakan and a Welfare member, over his Islamist activities.

The opposition proposal had sought a probe of remarks Kazan made suggesting members of the liberal Alevi Moslem sect take part in incestuous ceremonies and a visit he made to a Welfare mayor jailed for organising an Islamist protest also attended by Iran's ambassador.

The Hurriyet newspaper said members of coalition partner Tansu Ciller's party wanted to split the eight-month-old coalition straight away. But Ciller said she would not abandon the alliance. "No," she said when asked by reporters if she would quit the coalition.
The Milliyet daily had quoted Ciller, a pro-Western conservative, as telling her True Path Party on Monday she would desert Erbakan if he did not heed the influential army.
Erbakan attended last Friday's security meeting but the press says he refused to sign a council statement demanding an anti-Islamist crackdown.
"In a way he is challenging the state. He looks like he is rebelling against some of the rules of the democratic system," Anatolian news agency quoted leftist leader Bulent Ecevit as saying.
The National Security Council is legally charged with defending Turkey's official secularism. And political analysts say he ignores the generals at his peril.
The army, which often leads surveys as the country's most respected institution, has ousted three governments since 1960.

It virtually runs nine mainly-Kurdish provinces under emergency rule in the southeast where it has a free hand against separatist rebels. The armed forces also play a major role in Turkey's many disputes with neighbours Greece and Cyprus.
Young officers are taught to idolise Turkey's secularist founder Kemal Ataturk, himself a military man.
Health Minister Yildirim Aktuna, a member of Ciller's wing, predicted the prime minister could quit rather than disappoint his Islamist backers by heeding the army.
